problem.value: No live visibility into guest approval status at the door (people slip through or get wrongly turned away); freelancer invoices don't match hours worked; contracts often unsigned before the event; finance reconciles for weeks afterward.
problem.evidence: 'nobody has a clear view of who's actually been approved'; 'invoices never line up with hours actually worked'; 'half their contracts weren't even signed'

current_process.value: Freelancers manually check guests in at the door with no live approval reference; contracts frequently unsigned pre-event; finance manually reconciles invoices vs. worked hours weeks later.
current_process.evidence: As described in the request; no system in place today

existing_solutions.value: Not asked: nothing is in place today, but whether an off-the-shelf check-in or timesheet tool could cover the event inside six weeks, and the budget envelope, were never raised.
existing_solutions.evidence: This run predates the slot (issue 786); the request says nothing about buying, reusing or a budget.

success_metrics.value: Door staff see live approval status; someone is alerted on a mismatch; reconciliation is clean at close so finance stops chasing.
success_metrics.evidence: 'door staff should see approval status live... alerted when there's a mismatch... reconcile cleanly'

payer.evidence: This run predates the slot (issue 775). A commissioned system, not a product idea: it stays at its low baseline.

actors.value: Two actor sets: (1) attendees/guests being checked in, (2) freelancers acting as door staff whose own contracts/hours/invoices must reconcile. Finance and an unnamed alert recipient (event manager?) are downstream actors.
actors.evidence: 'freelancers to check guests in at the door'; 'finance spends weeks reconciling'

business_objects.value: Attendee (with approval status), Check-in event, Freelancer, Contract, Mission/shift, Hours worked, Invoice.
business_objects.evidence: Derived from request; no explicit data model stated

business_rules.value: Undefined: what makes a guest 'approved' and where that status originates; what exactly constitutes a 'mismatch' (guest count vs invoice? hours vs contract terms?); whether unsigned-contract freelancers may still work the door.
business_rules.evidence: Request names the pain but not the rule that decides approval or mismatch

workflow.value: Likely: guest registered/approved pre-event -> door staff check-in against approval list -> freelancer clocks in/out or hours logged -> post-event reconciliation of hours vs invoice vs signed contract -> alert on mismatch -> finance close.
workflow.evidence: Inferred from 'live approval status', 'alerted on mismatch', 'reconcile cleanly'

integrations.value: Unclear whether approval list, freelancer contracts and invoicing come from an existing HR/contract system (b2b-platform) that must feed this event app, or are entered fresh.
integrations.evidence: Not stated; finance reconciliation implies a source system exists somewhere

permissions.value: Door staff need read access to approval status only; someone (event manager/finance) needs to see and act on mismatch alerts; finance needs reconciliation view. Exact split not stated.
permissions.evidence: 'door staff should see approval status'; 'someone should get alerted' — 'someone' undefined

config_vs_custom.value: Not stated whether this is a one-off build for this single event or the first instance of a reusable kit for recurring events.
config_vs_custom.evidence: Event-ops context flags this as a question clients rarely raise themselves

constraints.value: Event in six weeks (hard, immovable deadline); venue wifi is effectively unusable, so the check-in path must work offline.
constraints.evidence: 'It has to work at the venue where the wifi basically doesn't. Event's in six weeks.'

edge_cases.value: Not addressed: walk-ins/last-minute approvals, duplicate/re-entry scans, multiple simultaneous doors, freelancer working partial shift or leaving early, unsigned contract at go-live.
edge_cases.evidence: Not mentioned; standard event-ops risk areas

reporting.value: Needs an auditable trail tying guest check-ins to freelancer hours to invoice lines, since finance's core complaint is inability to reconcile after the fact — this is close to a compliance/audit need, not just a nice dashboard.
reporting.evidence: 'finance spends weeks reconciling... invoices never line up with hours actually worked' implies a mandated traceable link

acceptance.value: Not defined: what scenario proves the system works (e.g., a live rehearsal check-in matching against approval list offline, then a mismatch alert firing correctly, then a clean reconciliation report)?

risks.value: Six-week timeline plus offline requirement plus fixing two intertwined problems (attendee check-in AND freelancer time/invoice reconciliation) is a lot to build and rehearse; risk of scope creep if both problems are solved with equal depth.
risks.evidence: Fixed event date + poor connectivity + dual scope (guests + freelancer ops) stated together

acquisition.evidence: This run predates the slot (issue 775). Used by the client's own door staff and finance, a known set of users: it stays at its low baseline.

questions.q: When you say 'alerted when there's a mismatch,' what exactly is being compared — guest check-ins against the approval list, or freelancer hours worked against contract/invoice terms (or both)? And who receives that alert?
questions.why: High impact, near-empty: the word 'mismatch' covers two very different rules (attendee approval vs. freelancer billing) with different data models and different owners — building the wrong one wastes most of the six weeks.

questions.q: Is the freelancer check-in/hours-tracking piece meant to reconcile against existing contracts and rates already in another system (e.g. an HR/contract platform), or will contracts and rates be entered fresh for this event?
questions.why: High impact, unaddressed: if a source-of-truth contract/invoicing system already exists, this is an integration and sync problem; if not, it's a much bigger build from scratch.

questions.q: Is this a one-off build for this single event, or the first version of a kit you'll reuse for future events?
questions.why: High impact on architecture and cost: a throwaway app vs. a reusable multi-event kit changes data model, configurability effort, and what's worth investing in given six weeks.

questions.q: For check-in itself: does the same 'approval' list also decide who is authorized to work the door (freelancer contract signed) — i.e., could an unsigned-contract freelancer still be scanning guests on the day?
questions.why: High impact: the request conflates guest approval and freelancer contract status; if an unsigned freelancer can still operate, that's a compliance gap the client may not have considered.

questions.q: On the offline requirement: do you need each door device to hold its own local snapshot of the approval list and sync check-ins later, and is a brief 'pending/unconfirmed' state on-screen acceptable during the event, or must every scan be instantly certain?
questions.why: High impact, high uncertainty: offline-first vs. online-only is an architecture decision, not a setting, and directly affects the failure mode at the door — the classic blind spot in event-ops builds.

questions.q: What does 'reconcile cleanly' mean concretely for finance — a report matching hours worked per freelancer against invoiced amounts, or full approval of invoices before payment? What's the acceptance scenario that proves this works?
questions.why: Medium-high impact: without a concrete acceptance definition, 'reconciles cleanly' can't be tested, and this is the metric the client explicitly cares about most for finance's sign-off.

summary.objective: Give door staff live, reliable visibility into guest approval status during check-in, and give finance a clean, auditable link between freelancer hours worked, signed contracts, and invoiced amounts — eliminating both wrongful admissions/rejections at the door and weeks of post-event invoice reconciliation.
summary.scope: Likely two connected sub-systems: (1) an offline-capable check-in app for door staff showing live attendee approval status, with local snapshot + sync given the venue's unreliable wifi; (2) a freelancer time/contract/invoice reconciliation layer that flags mismatches (hours vs. invoice vs. signed contract) and alerts a responsible person, feeding a clean reconciliation report to finance at close.
assumptions: The 'mismatch' alert covers both guest approval mismatches and freelancer hours-vs-invoice mismatches, though the client hasn't separated these explicitly.
An existing contract/HR/invoicing system may already hold freelancer contracts and rates, needing integration rather than fresh data entry.
The check-in path must work fully offline with local data snapshots and later sync, given the stated wifi problem.
This may be a one-off build for a single event in six weeks rather than a reusable kit, though this hasn't been confirmed.
Unsigned-contract freelancers are currently allowed to work the door, which the client wants addressed but hasn't explicitly ruled on.
summary.blind_spot: The request bundles two structurally different problems — attendee check-in (needing offline resilience, throughput, fuzzy identification) and freelancer contract/invoice reconciliation (needing traceable hours-to-invoice linkage, likely tied to another system of record) — under one word, 'mismatch.' Building a single undifferentiated alert without first separating these two rule sets risks solving neither well within six weeks, and the unsigned-contract-freelancer-at-the-door scenario is a compliance gap nobody has explicitly decided how to handle.

decisions.decision: The check-in path must work offline with a local device snapshot and later sync, given the venue's unreliable wifi.
decisions.why: The venue's connectivity is explicitly stated as unusable, and check-in cannot fail at the door.
decisions.alternative: An online-only check-in relying on live connectivity.
decisions.tradeoff: Added complexity of local snapshot freshness and sync conflict handling, in exchange for a check-in path that survives the one moment it can't fail.

decisions.decision: The event is being treated as its own scoped build within a fixed six-week deadline.

challenges.headline: One word, two different problems
challenges.premise: The request treats 'mismatch' as a single alert covering both guest approval and freelancer hours-vs-invoice discrepancies.
challenges.alternative: Event-ops and back-office reconciliation are structurally different builds — different data models, different urgency (real-time at the door vs. post-event for finance), different owners (door staff vs. finance).
challenges.consequence: Designing one undifferentiated 'mismatch' concept risks a shallow build that satisfies neither: a door alert that's too noisy to act on, and a finance report that still doesn't tie out.
challenges.recommendation: Split into two explicit rule sets and two acceptance criteria before writing any workflow — attendee approval mismatch, and hours/contract/invoice mismatch — each with its own owner and channel.

challenges.headline: Clocking freelancer hours is a legal tripwire
challenges.premise: The build assumes freelancer hours can simply be tracked and reconciled against invoices like a timesheet.
challenges.alternative: Under French labor law, freelancers who are clocked in/out and monitored like employees are a classic fact pattern for requalification as disguised employment (salariat déguisé) — freelance invoicing is normally tied to a deliverable or mission, not hours worked.
challenges.consequence: If the app effectively timestamps freelancer arrival/departure and drives invoice amounts from those hours, the client may be building evidence against their own contractor classification.
challenges.recommendation: Check with legal/HR before building an hours-based reconciliation — confirm whether the 'mismatch' should be against mission/deliverable terms in the contract, not clocked hours.

challenges.headline: Six weeks, two builds, no rehearsal slack
challenges.premise: The plan treats offline check-in and freelancer/invoice reconciliation as one project deliverable on the same six-week clock.
challenges.alternative: The event date can't move, so the check-in path — the one thing that fails visibly in front of the client — should get the depth and rehearsal time, while reconciliation could ship as a clean post-event report rather than a live alert.
challenges.consequence: Splitting effort evenly across both risks an under-rehearsed door experience, which is the one failure mode with no second chance.
challenges.recommendation: Sequence and scope explicitly: harden and rehearse check-in first; de-scope freelancer reconciliation to a post-event reconciliation report unless real-time alerting is proven necessary.

opportunities.text: Build the offline check-in engine (local snapshot + sync) as a reusable pattern for future events rather than a one-off, if the client runs events regularly.

Model the freelancer hours/contract/invoice reconciliation as an extension of the existing Mission-Contract-Invoice relationship rather than a bespoke event-specific check, so it can be reused across future freelance missions.
